title: Building Africa’s green industry from the ground up
body:
Walk through many African cities and you will see something powerful—and often underestimated:

Informal recyclers sorting plastics and metals

Repair technicians extending the life of appliances and electronics

Solar micro-distributors bringing clean energy to peri-urban communities

Circular economy entrepreneurs turning waste into value

At the SME level, the private sector is quietly enabling:

Material recovery

Product life extension

Clean energy access

Resource efficiency

Circular innovation

These activities are not marginal. They show that Africa’s green transition is already in motion. Yet most of these activities operate:

Informally

With low productivity

Without scale

Without affordable finance

Outside formal industrial policy frameworks

Any meaningful national green industrialization policy or strategy across the continent cannot afford to ignore these segments.

The real strategic question is not how to replace them, but how we can upgrade them. Why? Replacing them risks deepening unemployment and inequality.

Upgrading them, however, can drive the much-needed green industrialization on the continent.

So, what does upgrading these activities/segments mean in practice?

- Clear and gradual formalization pathways — not punitive enforcement
- Access to working capital and asset finance to scale up and facilitate risk sharing
- Cluster-based infrastructure (shared equipment, testing facilities, warehousing)
- Public procurement quotas for certified SMEs
- Technology upgrading and equipment support
- Skills development tied to market access
- Certification mechanisms that open doors to larger contracts
- Integration into larger anchor firms’ supply chains
- Digital platforms to improve market access and traceability

Africa’s green industrial future will not be built only in large industrial parks or mega-projects. It will also be built in workshops, repair hubs, waste aggregation centers, and small-scale assembly units.

**Bottom line:** If African countries ignore this layer, they deepen economic dualism: A modern green enclave on one side. A stagnant informal economy on the other.

But if they integrate and upgrade SMEs, they create dense industrial ecosystems. And dense ecosystems—not isolated projects—are what transform economies.

The difference between these futures and what Africa ends up with is policy design.

Africa’s green transition is already happening at the grassroots. The real question is whether policy will recognize it—and scale it.

Elvis K. Avenyo (Ph.D.) Solomon Owusu Victor Osei Kwadwo, Ph.D.Keyi Tang, Ph.D. Emmanuel Buadi Mensah Woubet Kassa
